JURISDICTION
The judgment of the court of appeals was entered on

denied on October 14, 2025 (Pet. App. 31a -32a).  The petition for a writ of certiorari was filed on January 12,
2026.  The jurisdiction of this Court rests on 28 U.S.C.
1254(1).
STATUTORY AND REGULATORY
PROVISIONS INVOLVED
Pertinent  statutory and regulatory provisions are
reproduced in the appendix to this brief.  App., infra,
1a-23a.
INTRODUCTION
The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C.
1101 et seq., authorizes the Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General, in his discretion , to “adjust
to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent
residence the status of any alien granted asylum” who
meets certain conditions.  8 U.S.C. 1159(b).  The question
presented is whether that provision applies to aliens
whose asylum status has been terminated.  The court of
appeals correct ly held that it does not.
When Congress bestows a benefit on an “alien granted
asylum,” the common -sense understanding is that the
benefit inures to an alien with asylum status, not to an y
alien who once had that status  but was later deprived of
it.  That is the way Congress used the same phrase in
defining the benefits accompanying asylum status in
8 U.S.C. 1158 , as petitioners acknowledge .  Congress
used the same phrase to the same effect when defining
an additional benefit in Section 1159(b).  The statutory
text and context both point in the same direction :  To adjust to the “status of an alien lawfully admitted  for permanent residence” under Section 1159(b), a n alien must,

3

at the time of adjustment, possess the “status of an[] alien
granted asylum”—i.e., asylum status.  8 U.S.C. 1159(b).
Petitioners’ contrary arguments require this Court to
accept the premise that Congress viewed the relevant distinction for eligibility for adjustment of status as whether
an alien has ever been granted asylum —regardless of
whether that status was revoked as mistaken or fraudulent, or was terminated due to criminal activity.  That
premise is unfounded.  Petitioners’ asserted  support
boils down to Congress’s use of a past participle  that can
sometimes function as a verb , what petitioners view as
clearer requirements of other continuing conditions elsewhere, and a series of unwarranted inferences  drawn
from other statutory provisions, statutory history, and
supposed congressional purpose.  None of those arguments, nor the rule of lenity , can overcome the force of
the plain statutory text  as reinforced by the relevant
context.  This Court should affirm  the decision below .
STATEMENT
A. Legal Background
The INA governs aliens’ admission to and removal
from the United States.  This case concerns provisions of
the INA  that were first enacted as part of the Refugee
Act of 1980  (Refugee Act), Pub. L. No. 96 -212, 94 Stat.
102.  The Refugee Act auth orizes certain forms of relief
for aliens who qualify as refugees, meaning that they are
facing persecution in their home countries because of
race, religion, nationality , membership in a particular social group, or political opinion .  8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) .
An alien outside of the United States who qualifies under that definition may apply for admission as a refugee, 8 U.S.C. 1157 (c), whereas an alien who is physically
present in the United States may apply for asylum ,
8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(1).

4

The Attorney General or the Secretary of Homeland
Security “may,” in his discretion, grant an alien asylum
status if the alien shows that he qualifies as a refugee
and does not fall into a disqualifying exception .  8 U.S.C.
1158(b)(1)(A) ; see 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2) and (b)(2 ).  An “alien granted asylum” may not be removed to his home
country, may work in the United States, and may be given
advance consent for travel abroad.  8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(1).
The spouse and children of an alien “granted asylum”
may “be granted the same status.”  8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(3)(A).
“Asylum granted   * * *  may be terminated ” for various reasons, including if the alien no longer qualifies as
a refugee, has committed a particularly serious crime,
is subject to removal to a third country pursuant to a
bilateral or multilateral agreement, has returned to
his home country, or has acquired a new nationality.
8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(2).  When asylum status is terminated,
the alien is subject to any applicable grounds of inadmissibility or deportability .  8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(3).  As
with the grant of asylum, termination is discretionary.
See 8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(2); In re K-A-, 23 I. & N. Dec. 661 ,
666 (B.I.A. 2004).
After an alien has been granted asylum, he may be
eligible for adjustment of status.  Under 8 U.S.C.
1159(b), the Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General , in his discretion and subject to additional regulations,  “may adjust to the status of an alien
lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of
any alien granted asylum” who meets certain conditions.  The alien must (1) apply for adjustment of status,
(2) have at least one year of physical presence in the
United States after being granted asylum, (3) continue
to be a refugee or a spouse or child of a refugee, (4) not
be firmly resettled in any foreign country, and (5)  be

5

admissible as an immigrant or qualify for a waiver of
inadmissibility described in 8 U.S.C. 1159(c).  8  U.S.C.
1159(b); see 8 C.F.R. 209.2, 1209.2.  Section 1159(c), in
turn, provides that certain grounds of inadmissibility
are inapplicable and allows the Secretary or the Attorney General to waive other grounds of inadmissibility
“for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity , or
when it is otherwise in the public interest.”  8  U.S.C.
1159(c).
B. Factual And Procedural Background
Petitioners are two aliens who were previously granted
asylum, had their asylum status terminated after convictions for particularly serious crimes, and were later
found ineligible for adjustment of status because of
their asylum termination s.
1. Petitioner Tamer Wassily, a native and citizen of
Egypt, entered the United States on a tourist visa in
1993.  Pet. App. 3a.  He remained here after the expiration of his authorized period of admission and was
placed in removal proceedings, in which he was granted
asylum by an immigration judge (IJ) in 2000.  See ibid.
In 2004, Wassily was convicted  of stalking in the third
degree and child endangerment , in violation of New
York state law .  Ibid.  Based on those convictions, the
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved to reopen his removal proceedings  and terminate his asylum
status.  Ibid.  In the reopened proceedings, the IJ concluded that Wassily’s stalking conviction was for a particularly serious crime,  terminated the previous grant
of asylum, and denied his renewed applications for asylum and related protection.   Id. at 69a-108a.  The Board
of Immigration Appeals (Board) dismissed Wassily’s
administrative appeal.  Id. at 62a-68a.  Among other
things, the Board rejected Wassily’s contention that his

6

former counsel was ineffective because he “fail[ed] to
request that [Wassily] be allowed to pursue adjustment
of status prior to termination of his asylee status.”  Id.
at 63a.
The court of appeals granted Wassily’s petition for
review and remanded to allow the agency to reconsider
whether Wassily had been convicted of a particularly
serious crime.  523 Fed. Appx. 783 .  The court also held
that the Board “did not adequately explain” its rejection
of Wassily’s ineffective -assistance claim.  Id. at 786.
The case was remanded to the IJ  and Wassily was permitted to file an application to adjust his status.  Administrative Record 695 .  On remand, the IJ again determined that the stalking offense constituted a particularly serious crime and that Wassily’s asylum status
was properly terminated.  Pet. App. 46a-50a.  But the IJ
also addressed Wassily’s application to adjust his status
and concluded that Wassily remained eligible to adjust to
lawful-permanent-resident status under 8 U.S.C. 1159(b),
despite the prior termination of his asylum status .  Pet.
App. 52a.  Although finding it an “extremely close case,”
the IJ proceeded to exercise discretion both to grant a
waiver of inadmissibility and to adjust his status .  Id. at
56a; see id. at 51a -58a.
On the government’s appeal, t he Board vacated the
IJ’s decision .  Pet. App. 33a-36a.  In doing so, the Board
relied on In re T-C-A-, 28 I. & N. Dec. 472 (B.I.A. 2022) ,
in which it had held that the best reading of Section
1159(b) allows only an alien who currently possess es
asylum status to adjust to lawful -permanent -resident
status.  See Pet. App. 35a .  Because Wassily’s asylum
status had previously been terminated, the Board vacated the IJ’s decision as to adjustment of status and
ordered Wassily ’s removal.  Id. at 36a.

7

Wassily then filed a petition for review with the Second Circuit.
b. Petitioner Byron Velasquez Arreaga, a native and
citizen of Guatemala, unlawfully entered the United
States in 1995 and was granted asylum the following
year.  Pet. App. 6a.  He later committed multiple criminal offenses, including those reflected in a 2015 conviction for driving while intoxicated and a 2018 conviction
for aggravated driving while intoxicated, both under
New York state law.  Ibid.
The 2018 conviction prompted DHS  to move to terminate Velasquez Arreaga’s asylum status and institute removal proceedings  against him.  Pet. App. 6a.  Concluding that the 2015 and 2018 convictions were, individually
and together , particularly serious crimes, an IJ terminated Velasquez Arreaga’s asylum status.  Id. at 6a-7a;
see id. at 136a .  Following the IJ’s decision, Velasquez
Arreaga indicated his intent to seek adjustment of status, but DHS filed a motion to pretermit that application, arguing that he was statutorily ineligible because
of the termination of his asylum status.  Id. at 7a.  The
IJ granted DHS’s motion, agreeing that only aliens with
current asylum status are eligible to adjust under Section 1159(b).  Id. at 135a-140a.  On appeal, the Board
affirmed the IJ’s decision regarding adjustment of status.  Id. at 121a -127a.  After a remand by the Second
Circuit on the collateral question of whether and when
the 2018 conviction became final, see id. at 116a -119a,
the Board ultimately  dismissed Velasquez Arreaga’s
appeal, id. at 109a-115a.
Velasquez Arreaga filed a petition for review with
the Second Circuit, which was consolidated with Wassily’s for purposes of argument and decision.   See Pet.
App. 2a.

8

2. a. The court of appeals denied both petitions .
Pet. App. 1a -30a.  The court held that the “more natural
reading” of the statutory phrase “  ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently
be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status .”  Id. at 12a.  The court explained that “ ‘the
ordinary meaning of “status” signals a present condition’
—in particular, a legal condition.”  Ibid. (quoting Cela
v. Garland, 75 F.4th 355, 364 (4th Cir. 2023), cert. denied,
144 S. Ct. 2657 (2024) ) (citation omitted) .  If present status were not important, the court observed , there would
have been no reason for Congress to use the term “status” at all.  Ibid.  The court found additional support for
its interpretation in a neighboring provision that “consistently uses ‘granted’ to refer to then -existing asylum
status,” id. at 13a (citing 8 U.S.C. 1158(c)) , and in a nother provision  that expressly permitted certain aliens
granted asylum before a certain date to apply for adjustment of status “ regardless of whether or not such
asylum has been terminated ,” id. at 17a (quoting Immigration Act of 1990, Pub. L. No. 101 -649, § 104(d)(1)(A),
104 Stat. 4985  (8 U.S.C. 1159 note) ) (emphasis omitted) .
The court of appeals rejected petitioners’ invocation
of other provisions of 8 U.S.C. 1159 that “use varying
language to require that a noncitizen seeking adjustment to lawful permanent resident status maintain
some other current condition.”  Pet. App. 14a.  The court
explained that those other provisions “cast no doubt ” on
Section 1159(b)’s clear language requiring “current asylum status.”  Id. at 15a.  Nor was the court persuaded
by petitioners’ reliance on the Attorney General’s discretion under Section 1159(c)  to waive grounds of inadmissibility that overlap in part with the grounds for terminating asylum.  Id. at 15a-16a.  Petitioners asserted

9

that, because of the overlap, the waiver provision would
have most effect in the context of aliens whose asylum
status had been terminated.  See ibid.  But the court
explained that the waiver authority is “not coextensive”
with the grounds for termination and the statute therefore “continues to vest the Secretary or Attorney General with discretion to waive the admissibility requirement, including in case s where an IJ defers ruling on a
motion to terminate asylum status in favor of first adjudicating an application for adjustment of status.”  Id. at
16a.
b. Judge Robinson dissented.  Pet. App. 19a -30a.
Although she considered this “a difficult case,” id. at
19a, she concluded that Section 1159(b) should not be
limited to aliens with current asylum status in light o f
Congress’s  use of the term “any alien granted asylum,”
id. at 20a (emphasis added), the other provisions imposing continuing requirements , id. at 21a -24a, and what
she viewed as an “incongruous result” for the waiver
provision , id. at 29a.
c. The court of appeals denied rehearing en banc.
Pet. App. 31a -32a.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Congress has authorized the Secretary  or the Attorney General to “adjust to the status of an alien lawfully
admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum” who meets certain conditions.
8 U.S.C. 1159(b).  That provision does not apply to aliens
whose asylum status has already been terminated.
A. Reading Section 1159(b) to apply only to aliens
with current asylum status is consistent with the statutory text and context.  The word “granted” is a past  participle that can refer either to a completed action or to
a present state.  Here, the full statutory phrase indi-

10

cates the latter.  Section 1159(b) contemplates the alien’s transition from one status (that of an “alien granted
asylum” ) to another  (that of an “alien lawfully admitted
for permanent residence” ).  The alien must be in the
first status in order to adjust to the second.
The immediate statutory context confirms that Congress used the phrase “alien granted asylum” to refer
to the alien’s present status.  In a neighboring section,
Congress identified benefits available to an “alien granted
asylum,” including protection from removal and work
authorization.  8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(1).  Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.
The opportunity to apply for adjustment of status is another benefit  that likewise  ceases when an alien is no
longer “granted asylum.”  And a 1990 amendment to
Section 1159 confirms the point.  Congress enacted a separate provision that permits “[c]ertain [f ]ormer [a]sylees”
to adjust their status under Section 1159(b) “regardless
of whether or not such asylum has been terminated.”
8 U.S.C. 1159 note.  That express exception for a limited
class of aliens whose asylum status ha s been terminated
indicates that Section 1159(b) generally does not permit
adjustment for those who have lost their asylum status .
B. Petitioners’ contrary arguments are unpersuasive.  On the text, they argue that the word “granted ”
indicates a past event, but they ultimately acknowledge
that Congress used the same phrase in Section 1158(c)(1)
to refer to someone with continuing asylum status.  The
inclusion of other continuing requirements using different wording in other parts of Section 1159 does not cast
doubt on the phras e that Congress used in both Sections
1158(c)(1) and 1159(b) to refer to continuing asylum status.  And contrary to petitioners’ contention, the Attorney
General’s statutory authority to waive certain grounds of

11

inadmissibility when adjusting  an alien’s status  retains
its force under the government’s reading .  The statutory regime simply requires an exercise of discretion
not to terminate an alien’s asylum if there is a desire to
exercise th e discretionary waiver authority .
The statutory history and purpose provide no support for petitioners’ preferred interpretation.  Petitioners highlight t he text of a separate adjustment -of-status
provision  that was superseded decades before Section
1159’s enactment and that sheds no light on its meaning.
They erroneously assert that the current-asylum requirement would have done no work when Section 1158
was first enacted.  And they rely on their incorrect understanding of the Attorney General’s waiver authority
in attempting to show that Congress intended that some
former asylees remain eligible for adjustment.
Finally, petitioners’ last -resort appeal to lenity is
misplaced.  In the immigration context, that rule applies
only to grievous ambiguities in deportation statutes.
Section 1159(b) is neither a deportation statute nor ambiguous.
ARGUMENT
ADJUSTMENT OF STATUS UNDER 8 U.S.C. 1159( b) IS
AVAILABLE ONLY  TO ALIENS WITH ASYLUM STATUS
In the Refugee Act, Congress authorized the  Secretary or the  Attorney General , in his discretion, to “adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum” who meets certain conditions.  8 U.S.C. 1159(b).  Petitioners do not qualify for that discretionary benefit  because the termination of their asylum status means that
they are no longer “alien [s] granted asylum.”

12

A. The Statutory Text And Context  Confirm  That Section
1159(b) Limit s Adjustment Of Status To Aliens With
Asylum Status
The court of appeals correctly held that the phrase
“the status of any alien granted asylum” is most naturally read as referring to an alien with asylum status.
8 U.S.C. 1159(b); see Pet. App. 12a.  That reading is supported by the statutory text and context.
1. Under the plain text of Section 1159(b), “the status of
any alien granted asylum” refers to an alien with
asylum status
In determining whether petitioners are eligible for
adjustment of status under Section 1159(b), the critical
statutory phrase is “the status of any alien granted asylum.”  8 U.S.C. 1159(b).  The word “granted” is a past
participle .  As this Court has recognized, a past participle may indicate “past or completed action ,” Florida
Dep’t of Revenue v. Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc. , 554 U.S.
33, 39 (2008), or it may be used as an “adjective [] to describe the present state of a thing,” Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc. , 582 U.S. 79, 84 (2017).  See
Bryan A. Garner, Garner’s Modern English Usage  1229
(5th ed. 2022).
“Widening [the] view to take in the statutory phrase”
reveals whether Congress used the term  to describe a
historical event or a present state .  Henson, 582 U.S. at
84.  The language of Section 1159(b) is focused on the
“status of any alien granted asylum.”  8 U.S.C. 1159(b)
(emphasis added) .  Status is defined as a person’s “legal
relation  * * *  to the rest of the community,” and includes
the “rights, duties, capacities, and incapacities  which determine a person to a given class.”  Black’s Law Dictionary  1264 (5th ed. 1979); see American Heritage
Dictionary 1260 (1980) (“The legal character or condi-

13

tion of a person or thing”); Webster’s Third New International Dictionary  2230 (1976) (“[T]he condition (as
arising out of  * * *  alienage  * * * )  of a person that determines the nature of his legal personality, his legal  capacities, and the nature of the legal relations to the state
or to other persons into which he may enter”).  As the
court of appeals recognized, “the ordinary meaning of
‘status’ signals a present condition.”  Pet. App. 12a (quoting Cela v. Garland, 75 F.4th 355, 364 (4th Cir. 2023),
cert. denied, 144 S. Ct. 2657 (2024)).
Section 1159(b) plainly us es “status” in its ordinary,
present sense.  The statute permits the Attorney General to “adjust”  (or “change,” American Heritage Dictionary 16) an alien’s status  from one condition  (the
“status of an[] alien granted asylum” ) to another  (the
“status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence” ), 8 U.S.C. 1159(b).  Congress thus used parallel
structure to identify the two statuses by means of the
conferring event.  Just as the “status of an alien lawfully
admitted for permanent residence” is lawful -permanentresident status, see 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(20), the “status of
any alien granted asylum” is asylum status.  And in authorizing an adjustment from one status to the other,
Section 1159(b) requires that the alien be in the first
status at the time of the potential adjustment.
Congress manifestly knows how to provide aliens
with immigration benefits that are not conditioned on
present status.  In 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(1), for example, Congress provided that “[a]ny alien who is physically present
in the United States  *  * * ,  irrespective of such  alien’s
status, may apply for asylum.”  And in two subsections
of 8 U.S.C. 1255, Congress provided for adjustment of
an alien’s status “to that of an alien lawfully admitted
for permanent residence” without identifying the alien’s

14

prior status as part of the threshold eligibility.  Section
1255(a) provides threshold eligibility for adjustment of
status for “an alien who was inspected and admitted or
paroled into the United States” who meets certain conditions, 8 U.S.C. 1255(a), and Section 1255(i) extends
threshold eligibility to “an alien physically present in
the United Statues” under certain circumstances,
8 U.S.C. 1255(i)(1).  If Congress had wanted to allow all
aliens who have ever been granted asylum to be eligible
for adjustment of status, without regard to their current status, it could have specified that adjustment was
available “irrespective of status ” or defined an alien’s
threshold eligibility without invoking the alien’s initial
status at all.  That Congress did not do so in Section
1159(b) indicates that it did not intend that result.
Nor is it unusual for Congress to have used the past
participle “granted” as an adjective describing a present state  in Section 1159(b) .  It has used the same formulation , for example, when imposing conditions on
“[p]ersons granted authority to make arrests,” 51 U.S.C.
20134; when requiring a “person granted an exemption”
from certain requirements to demonstrate continued
compliance with conditions, 21 U.S.C. 360j(m)(5) ; and
when providing that “[e]ach person granted a customs
broker’s license” shall receive certain permits, 19 U.S.C.
1641(c)(1).  In each of those instance s, Congress used
the past participle , and it would make little sense to
read those provisions as imposing requirements or benefits that persist even after  the “granted” authorit ies,
exemption s, or license s have lapsed .
Common usage likewise confirms that past participles are used to refer to present conditions rather than
a previous status that has since been rescinded.  If a
university announced that any person granted an hon-

15

orary degree was invited to a celebratory dinner, no one
would expect that invitation to extend to an individual
whose honorary degree was revoked.  If this Court
stated that any lawyer admitted  to the Supreme Court
Bar may sit in the bar section during oral argument, all
would understand that a disbarred attorney would be
turned away.  And, to adapt an example recently used
by the Court,  if the U.S. Olympic Committee enacted a
rule that any athlete awarded  an Olympic gold medal
could be called an Olympi c Champion , an athlete who
had been stripped of her medal could no  longer claim
that title.  Cf. Hewitt v. United States , 606 U.S. 419, 428-
429 (2025).  As in those common-usage examples , Section 1159(b) grants a particular privilege to a group defined by a particular status.  When that status is terminated, the privilege is no longer available.
2. The immediate statutory context confirms that Section 1159(b) refers to aliens with asylum status
The immediate statutory context of Section 1159(b)
provides strong indications that Congress used the
phrase “alien granted asylum” to reach only those with
current asy lum status .  The same phrase is undisputedly used to that effect in a neighboring section of the
INA, and Congress enacted a limited exception allow ing
only certain aliens whose asylum status has been terminated to apply for adjustment under Section 1159(b).
a. In the section of the INA governing  grants of asylum, 8 U.S.C. 1158, Congress set out who is eligible to
apply for asylum, the conditions for granting asylum,
and what benefits accompany asylum status.  The subsection with the heading “[a]sylum status” provides that
“[i]n the case of an alien granted asylum   * * * ,  the
Attorney General” “shall not remove” the alien  to his
home country, “shall authorize the alien to engage in

16

employment,” and may grant “prior consent” to “ allow
the alien to travel abroad .”  8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(1) (A)-(C)
(emphasis added) .  The next paragraph further provides
that “[a]sylum granted  * * *  may be terminated” in certain circumstances .  8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(2).  Terminati on of
asylum results in the termination of the benefits listed
in Section 1158(c)(1).  See 8 U.S.C. 1158(c)(3) (providing
that an alien whose asylum status has been terminated
“is subject to any applicable grounds  of inadmissibility
and deportability” and may be removed in accordance

Nor does the presence of a continuing -asylum requirement render superfluous  the additional requirement that the alien “continues to be a refugee .”  8 U.S.C.
1159(b).  Because the termination of asylum status has
always been within the discretion of the Attorney General, an alien may continue to be “granted asylum” even
when he ceases to qualify as a refugee.  Congress has
provided the Attorney General with the discretion not
to terminate asylum status in such circumstances , but it
has not further permitted an adjustment to lawful -
permanent -resident status under Section 1159(b).
As petitioners recognize (Br. 31), Congress broadened the statutory grounds for terminating asylum in
1996.  See Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant
Responsibility Act of 1996  (IIRIRA) , Pub. L. No. 104-
208, § 604(a), 110 Stat. 3009-692 to 3009 -693.  Petitioners nevertheless object (Br. 32) that , under the government’s interpretation, Section 1 159(b)’s threshold requirement of asylum status increased in importance
when the additional bases for termination were enacted .
With each additional ground for termination, petitioners explain, more aliens could have their status terminated and then be come ineligible to adjust their status.
Petitioners believe (ibid.) that “Congress would not
have made such a significant change without saying a
word.”
But Congress actually said many words when making that change.  It expressly added each of the additional bases for terminati ng asylum .  And just six years
earlier, Congress had enacted the 1990 Act, in which

34

Congress made evident that it was aware of the effect
that termination of asylum would have on the ability to
adjust status.  See pp. 17-19, supra.  When Congress
expanded the grounds for termination in 1996, it could
have altered the threshold condition for adjustment of status, just as it had done for “[c]ertain [f  ]ormer [a]sylees”
in the 1990 Act.  § 104(d), 104 Stat. 4985 (8 U.S.C. 1159
note).  But it chose not to do so.  No additional words were
required to effectuate the desired change.
In any event, petitioners overstate the change s that
IIRIRA made with respect to termination of asylum
status.  Ever since the Attorney General adopted interim regulations implementing Section 1158 in 1980,
regulations have provided for the termination or revocation of asylum status based on a “conviction of a serious crime.”  8 C.F.R. 208.15 (a)(2) (1981); see 45 Fed.
Reg. 37,392 (June 2, 1980).  Regardless of whether petitioners view those regulations as consistent with the
statutory language , they formed part of the backdrop
when Congress amended the statutory bases for termination in 1996 .  See 8 C.F.R. 208.14(d)(1), 208.24(a)(3)
(1995).  Congress therefore would have been aware that
additional statutory grounds for termination would not
constitute a “sea change. ”  Pet. Br. 32 (citation omitted).
4. Petitioners’ interpretation is not necessary to
achieve Congress’s purposes
Petitioners contend that their interpretation is more
consistent with the statutory purpose.  But in doing so,
they suggest barriers to the statute’s operation that do
not exist .  Adjustment s to lawful -permanent -resident
status under Section 1159 (b) can continue to operate as
Congress intended without being made available to former asylees .

35

a. Petitioners once again invoke (Br. 36 -38) the Attorney General’s waiver authority in contending that
Congress did not intend to foreclose adjustment of status
for all aliens whose asylum status has been terminated.
That argument suffers from the same flaws as petitioners’ contextual argument relying on the same waiver provision.  See pp. 24-25, supra.  By ignoring the Attorney
General’s discretion when deciding whether to terminate
asylum, petitioners draw unsupported inferences.  Permitting the Attorney General to waive grounds for inadmissibility that overlap with grounds for asylum termination indicates that Congress did not intend to foreclose adjustment to every alien whose asylum status
could be terminated.  But it does not follow that Congress further intended to allow adjustment for those
whose asylum status actually has  been terminated.
An alien’s asylum status may be subject to termination for reasons “entirely outside [his] control ,” Pet. Br.
36, or based on criminal conduct that is “relatively minor,” id. at 37 .  If so, those factors may weigh against
the Attorney General ’s exercise of discretion to terminate asylum. Where the Attorney General decides not
to terminate asylum , Congress has left open a pathway
to citizenship in some instances .  See In re  K-A-, 23
I. & N. Dec. 661, 662 ( B.I.A. 2004) (dismissing appeal of
IJ decision declining to terminate alien’s asylum status
and adjusting her status based on the hardship her removal would cause to her “severely disabled United
States citizen child”).  But the Attorney General may
also exercise discretion to decide  that, despite potentially sympathetic circumstances, termination of asylum
is warranted.  That discretion may be exercised on an
individualized basis when taking into consideration an
alien’s particular circumstances, or by regulation as in

36

the case of derivative asylees.  See 8 C.F .R. 1208.24(d)
(terminating derivative asylum status automatically
upon the termination of the principal applicant’s asylum
status).  Where the Attorney General concludes that
asylum should be terminat ed, no congressional purpose
is thwarted by precluding that alien from seeking adjustment of status under Section 1159(b).
Petitioner Wassily’s circumstances do not suggest
otherwise.  In his case, the IJ —using authority delegated from the Attorney General, see 8 C.F.R. 1003.10,
1208.24(f  ), 1245.2(a)(1)(i) —terminated Wassily’s asylum status before considering his application to adjust
status (while operating under  the mistaken belief that
continuing asylum status was unnecessary at that
point).  See Pet. App. 52a.  Of course, t he Court’s resolution of this case will prevent such a mistake from being repeated  in the future.  But even for Wassily, the
IJ’s error was no bar to the Attorney General’s exercise
of discretion.  If he had wished to do so, he could have
directed the Board to refer the case to him and exercised his own discretion to decline to terminate
Wassily’s asylum status before adjusting his status  to
that of a lawful permanent resident .  See 8 C.F.R.
1003.1(h)(1) (i) (requiring the Board to refer to the Attorney General all cases that “ [t]he Attorney General
directs the Board to refer to him”).  That the Attorney
General has the ultimate discretion and must exercise
that discretion consistently across the two decisions
does not “make[] nonsense of the statutory scheme.”
Pet. Br. 39.  It simply indicates that Congress reasonably expected the Executive to harmonize its various interests when exercising both forms of discretion.
b. Petitioners likewise miss the mark in contending
(Br. 38) that precluding former asylees from adjusting

37

status under Section 1159(b) would afford them “less
protection than their refugee counterparts ,” who may
adjust status under Section 1159(a).   According to petitioners (ibid.), for aliens admitted as refugees as well as
those granted asylum, the focus when considering eligibility for adjustment of status should be on whether
they have a “well -founded fear of persecution”  (and
therefore continue to be refugees).
Even under petitioners’ interpretation of “alien
granted asylum,” however, the availability of adjustment to refugees and asylees would not be the same.
For the former, “refugee status” may be terminated
only when “the alien was not in fact a refugee  *  * *  at
the time of the alien’s admission.”  8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4) ;
see 8 C.F.R. 207.9.  But a n alien who is admitted as a
refugee does not have to continue to qualify as a refugee
at the time of adjustment.  8 U.S.C. 1159(a).  Thus, i f
country conditions changed in the intervening year between his admission as a refugee and his return to DHS
for adjustment of status, that would not be a basis for
terminating his refugee status or for declining to adjust
his status to that of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residenc e.  By contrast, an “alien[] granted asylum” is not eligible to adjust status unless he “continue s
to be a refugee .”  8 U.S.C. 1159(b)(3).
More fundamentally, Congress designed the statutory framework  that treats those with refugee status
and those with asylum status differently  in certain respects.  Congress decided to allow for termination of
asylum status in more circumstances than refugee status.  And Congress imposed requirements for adjustment for “ aliens granted asylum” in Section 1159(b)
that it did not impose for refugees  in Section 1159(a) .

38

Such policy choices are for Congress alone.  See Patel,
596 U.S. at 346.
5. Resort to the immigration rule of lenity is unwarranted
Petitioners finally resort (Br. 40 -44) to lenity , citing
the “long standing principle of construing any lingering
ambiguities in deportation statutes in favor of the alien.”  INS v. St. Cyr , 533 U.S. 289, 320 (2001) (quoting
Cardoza -Fonseca, 480 U.S. at 449).  That argument
fails.
a. As an initial matter, the principle that petitioners
cite does not apply because Section 1159 is not a deportation statute.  The principle is grounded in this Court’s
reasoning that “deportation is a drastic measure and at
times the equivalent of banishment or exile,” such that
the Court “will not assume that Congress meant to
trench on [an alien’s] freedom beyond that which is required by the narrowest of the several possible meanings of the words used.”  Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333
U.S. 6, 10 (1948) ; see INS v. Errico, 385 U.S. 214, 225
(1966).  The Court thus expects Congress to speak with
added clarity when dealing with the serious matter of
deportation.
In allowing certain aliens granted asylum to adjust
their status to that of a lawful permanent resident, Section 1159 (b) does not deal with deportation .  Instead, it
provides a discretionary immigration benefit that is a
step along the path to citizenship.  See 8 U.S.C. 1427(a)
(conditioning naturalization in part on an alien residing
continuously in the United States for at least five years
after “being lawfully admitted for permanent residence”); see also Pet. App. 13a -14a.  When such benefits
are at issue, this Court has at times construed any ambiguity in favor of the government.  See Swan & Finch

39

Co. v. United States , 190 U.S. 143, 146 (1903) (holding
that where a “governmental grant of a privilege or benefit” is at issue, “it is to be construed in favor of the government and against the party claiming the grant”);
United States  v. Manzi, 276 U.S. 463, 467 (1928) (applying that principle to a grant of citizenship).
Petitioners nevertheless contend (Br. 43) that this
Court has applied the lenity principle beyond deportation statutes to “provisions that bear on whether a non -
citizen will or will not be removed.”  But the examples
they cite involved statutes that were directly connected
to deportation or removal proceedings.  In Errico, for
example, the statute involved an express waiver of deportation for certain aliens.  385 U.S. at 215.  St. Cyr
involved a statute that had been interpreted to authorize certain aliens “to apply for a discretionary waiver
from deportation.”  533 U.S. at 295.  And in Dada v.
Mukasey , 554 U.S. 1 (2008), the Court considered the
interaction between “the statutory right to file a motion
to reopen in removal proceedings” and the “rules governing voluntary departure” when requested at the conclusion of removal proceedings.  Id. at 8; see id. at 8-9.
Section 1159(b)’s connection to removal is far more
attenuated.  Nothing in the text of Section 1159 (b) expressly  connects it to removal , and it regularly operates
wholly outside the context of removal proceedings.  Under petitioners ’ logic, the rule of lenity would apply to
any provision authorizing immigration benefits that
could prevent removal—including naturalization provisions.  U.S. citizenship is the ultimate protection against
removal, and aliens with lawful -permanent -resident
status may attempt to naturalize to avoid removal proceedings, just as petitioners here sought to adjust  their
status.  See, e.g., In re Hidalgo , 24 I. & N. Dec. 103, 107-

40

108 (B.I.A. 2007) ( recognizing that an IJ may terminate
removal proceedings if DHS provides “affirmative communication regarding the [alien’s] prima facie eligibility
for naturalization”) .  Yet that would run counter to this
Court’s recognition that “[c]itizenship is a high privilege, and when doubts exist concerning a grant of it,
generally at least, they should be resolved in favor of
the United States.”  Manzi, 276 U.S. at 467.  The Court
should therefore decline to extend the rule of lenity to
this context.
b. In all events, “even assuming that the rule of lenity can be invoked in this particular civil immigration
context, the rule applies only if after seizing everything
from which aid can be derived, there remains grievous
ambiguity.”  Pugin v. Garland , 599 U.S. 600, 610 (2023)
(citation and internal quotation marks omitted) .  Because the traditional tools of statutory interpretation
are sufficient to conclude that “the status of any alien
granted asylum” refers to an alien with current asylum
status, there is no basis for resorting to lenity.  See ibid.

41

CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be affirmed.

4. 8 C.F.R. 208.8(f  ) (1981)  provide d:
Decision by the district director.
Denial —(1) General.  The district director shall deny
a request for asylum or extension of asylum status if it
is determined that the alien:
(i)  Is not a refugee  within the meaning of
section 101(a)(42) of the Act;
(ii)  Has been firmly resettled in a foreign
country;
(iii) That the alien ordered, incited, assisted
or otherwise participated in the persecution of any
person on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular group, or political opinion;
(iv) The alien, having been convicted by a final judgment of a particularly serious crime, constitutes a danger to the community of the United States;
(v)  There are serious reasons for considering
that the alien has committed a serious non -political
crime outside the United States prior to the arrival
of the alien in the United States; or
(vi) There are reasonable g rounds for regarding the alien as a danger to the security of the
United States.
(2) Discretion .  Among other grounds, the district
director may deny a request for asylum or extension of
asylum status in the exercise of discretion if it is deter-

mined that there is an outstanding offer of resettlement
by a third nation where the applicant will not be subject
to persecution and the applicant ’s resettlement in a
third nation is in the public interest.
(3) Applicant for admission .  If an asylum request
by an applicant for admission is denied, he/she shall be
expeditiously placed under exclusion proceedings, unless the applicant elects to withdraw the application for
admission.
(4) Applicant in the United States .  If a request for
asylum or extension of asylum by an alien in the United
States is denied, the district director may in his discretion, grant voluntary departure pursuant to O.I. 242.10,
or commence deportation proceedings pursuant to
8 CFR 242.1.

6. 8 C.F.R. 208.14(d) (1995)  provide d:
Approval, denial, or referral of application.
Mandatory denials .  An application for asylum shall
be denied if:
(1) The alien, having been convicted by a final judgment of a particularly serious crime in the United
States, constitutes a danger to the community;
(2) The applicant has been firmly resettled within
the meaning of § 208.15;
(3) There are reasonable grounds for regarding the
alien as a danger to the security of the United States; or
(4) The alien has been convicted of an aggravated
felony, as defined in section 101(a)(43) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(43).

exclusive procedure for adjustment of status by an

asylee admitted under section 208 of the Act whose application is based on his or her asylee status.
(a) Eligibility .  (1) Except as provided in paragraph
(a)(2) or (a)(3) of this section, the status of any alien who
has been granted asylum in the United States may be

and (vi) has a refugee number available under section
207(a) of the Act.

exceeds the refugee numbers available under section
207(a) of the Act for the fiscal year, a waiting list will be
established on a priority basis by the date the application was properly filed.
